justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline across all three horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to recent price action and momentum, assuming no major overnight catalysts would materially shift the market. The slight upward drift from the current level reflects the general tendency of equity markets to grind higher in the absence of negative shocks, as well as any near-term technical support levels I weighted in. For the one-week estimate, I extended that drift modestly further, incorporating a slight mean-reversion pull alongside continued positive momentum. The one-month estimate steps up again, reflecting the longer-term upward bias in equity prices, expected earnings growth, and the assumption that macro conditions remain broadly supportive without a significant deterioration in rate expectations or credit conditions.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the range is relatively tight because intraday and overnight volatility is fairly bounded under normal conditions, and most information is already priced in. At one week, I widened the interval to account for scheduled macro releases, Federal Reserve communications, and the possibility of unexpected geopolitical developments. At one month, the interval is quite wide because a full month encompasses earnings announcements, inflation data, employment reports, and potential shifts in central bank guidance — any of which could independently move markets by several percent in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise hawkish pivot from the Federal Reserve, a significant deterioration in corporate earnings guidance, or an escalation in geopolitical conflict could push prices well below my lower bounds. A sudden liquidity event or credit market stress — such as a major financial institution facing distress — would also represent a tail risk not fully captured in my intervals. On the upside, a faster-than-expected decline in inflation data, strong labor market resilience paired with cooling wage growth, or a positive surprise on earnings could push prices above my upper bounds. I would also note that my intervals assume relatively normal market functioning; in conditions of extreme volatility or illiquidity, realized outcomes could fall outside even the stated 90% confidence range.
